God put Christ forward as the propitiation: God Himself provided what God required. The Judge supplied the satisfaction that the guilty could not provide. This is the gospel's internal logic: God's justice demanded penalty; God's love supplied the penalty-bearer; God's grace declared the guilty ones righteous on the basis of the One who bore their guilt. Faith receives what grace provides.

verseByVerse.ref: Not by Works of the Law
verseByVerse.quote: ...yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified. — Galatians 2:16
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul states the negative three times in a single verse — "not by works of the law" — with an emphasis that suggests he is contending against a deeply rooted contrary assumption. The occasion was Peter's withdrawal from table fellowship with Gentile believers at Antioch (v.12), which implicitly required Gentile Christians to adopt Jewish practices in order to be fully accepted. Paul saw that this struck at the root of the gospel: if even one additional requirement is added to faith in Christ as the basis of justification, the gospel is lost.

The principle Paul enunciates is absolute: "by works of the law no one will be justified" — not merely no Gentiles, not merely those who try particularly hard, but no one. The law cannot justify because it can only reveal sin (Rom 3:20), produce wrath (Rom 4:15), and condemn the guilty (Gal 3:10). It cannot provide the righteousness it demands. Only faith in Christ — faith in the One who kept the law perfectly and bore its curse — can provide what the law requires and we cannot produce. Luther's comment is apt: the law says "do this" and it is never done; the gospel says "believe this" and everything is already done.

verseByVerse.quote: For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God. — 2 Corinthians 5:21
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is perhaps the most compressed and most magnificent statement of the atonement and justification in all of Scripture. The exchange is total and mutual: Christ took what was ours (sin), we receive what is His (righteousness). He "knew no sin" — the sinlessness of the substitute is the presupposition of the exchange. A sinful substitute would be paying his own debt, not ours. Only the truly innocent One can stand in the guilty one's place and make the exchange valid.

He was "made sin" — not made a sinner in His inner being, but made to bear the weight, the guilt, the penalty of sin. At Calvary, God treated Christ as if He had lived our sinful lives, so that He might treat us as if we had lived Christ's righteous life. And the result: "we might become the righteousness of God" — not merely be forgiven our sins, but receive a positive righteousness, be clothed in the perfect obedience of the Son, be counted as righteous as the One who died in our place. Imputed righteousness is not a legal fiction; it is the deepest justice — a justice that required a cross to accomplish and leaves the redeemed breathless with gratitude forever.

8.title: The Authority of Scripture
8.overview:
The Reformation was ignited by a dispute about authority. Luther's famous words at the Diet of Worms — "My conscience is captive to the Word of God" — announced a principle that would reshape Western Christianity: the Bible, and not the church or its traditions, is the supreme authority in all matters of faith and practice. This principle — sola scriptura, Scripture alone — is the formal principle of the Reformation, the epistemological foundation on which all its doctrinal conclusions rest.

The doctrine of Scripture's authority rests on two foundational claims: its divine origin (inspiration) and its divine purpose (sufficiency). On inspiration: the Bible is not merely a human record of religious experience but the very Word of God, breathed out by the Spirit through human authors who wrote genuinely and freely, but whose writing was so superintended by the Spirit that what they wrote is what God intended to say. On sufficiency: the Bible contains everything necessary for salvation and godliness — we do not need supplementary revelation, magisterial tradition, or continuing prophecy to know what God requires and what He has provided.

Reformed theology's doctrine of Scripture has always included a doctrine of Scripture's self-authentication: the Bible does not derive its authority from the church that endorses it or the scholars who analyze it. It carries its own authority because it is God's word, and the Spirit illumines the believer to perceive that authority as it truly is. This is what Calvin called the testimonium Spiritus Sancti internum — the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit — which gives the believer a settled, certain confidence in the Word of God that transcends all external arguments for its authority.
8.theology:
Inspiration: Verbal and Plenary

Reformed theology has defended a doctrine of verbal, plenary inspiration: verbal (the inspiration extends to the actual words of Scripture, not merely the ideas), and plenary (the inspiration extends to all parts of Scripture equally, not merely the "spiritual" or "religious" parts). This does not mean that God dictated the Bible word for word — the human authors wrote in their own styles, drew on their own experiences, and expressed their own personalities. But the Spirit so guided the process that the result is what God intended: words that are, in the words of the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy, "without error in all that they affirm."

The Canon

Reformed theology has understood the canon of Scripture — the sixty-six books of the Old and New Testaments — as the complete, closed deposit of divine revelation. The canon is not a human invention that gives authority to the books within it; rather, the church recognized and received books that carried self-evident divine authority. The Westminster Confession's statement is careful: we believe the Scriptures to be the Word of God "not because of the testimony of any man or church, but wholly upon God (who is truth itself) the author thereof: and therefore it is to be received, because it is the Word of God."

Sufficiency and Clarity

Two important corollaries of scriptural authority: sufficiency (the Bible contains all we need for salvation and godliness, so that no additional revelation is required) and clarity, or perspicuity (the main things of Scripture are sufficiently clear that ordinary believers can understand them, though not all things are equally clear). These two doctrines protect the church from two opposite errors: adding to Scripture (by means of tradition, prophecy, or papal decree) and treating Scripture as a mystery accessible only to experts.
8.examples:
Then: The medieval church had, in practice, elevated tradition and papal authority to a level equal to or above Scripture. The faithful could not read the Bible in their own language; interpretation was reserved for the clergy; and doctrines with no scriptural basis (indulgences, purgatory, the treasury of merit) had become established dogma. The Reformers' recovery of sola scriptura was therefore not an innovation but a return — a demand that Christian doctrine and practice be tested by the standard of the written Word rather than by the accumulated weight of ecclesiastical tradition.

Now: The authority of Scripture is under pressure from both outside and inside the church. Outside: postmodern epistemology questions whether any text can have a fixed, determinable meaning — the reader constructs meaning, and no reading is privileged over another. Inside: many evangelical churches have subtly shifted from Scripture as the supreme authority to experience, therapeutic categories, or cultural accommodation. The recovery of a robust doctrine of Scripture — including its inspiration, authority, sufficiency, and clarity — is the most urgent theological need of the contemporary church.

verseByVerse.quote: All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work. — 2 Timothy 3:16–17
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Breathed out by God" — the Greek word is theopneustos (theo = God, pneustos = breathed). The metaphor is of exhalation: just as God breathed into Adam's nostrils and he became a living being (Gen 2:7), God breathed out the Scriptures and they became the living Word. The direction of breath is from God outward — Scripture is not a human document that God then authorized, but a divine document that God produced through human instrumentality.

The scope is total: "all Scripture" — not some particularly inspired portions, not only the red letters, not only the New Testament, but every word in every book. And the purpose is comprehensive: teaching (giving true doctrine), reproof (identifying error and sin), correction (restoring the fallen), training in righteousness (discipling the growing). The result: "the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work." Complete — not lacking anything, not needing supplementary revelation, not requiring additional sources. The sufficiency of Scripture is the sufficiency of God's own speech for human flourishing. The Bible does not merely assist us toward godliness; it is the sufficient, complete, all-equipping instrument of the Spirit for producing it.

verseByVerse.quote: ...and Scripture cannot be broken... — John 10:35
verseByVerse.commentary:
This brief phrase, embedded in a larger argument, reveals Jesus's view of Scripture with breathtaking clarity. He is arguing from a Psalm (82:6), and His argument rests on a single word in the text. To justify this level of precision, He adds: "and Scripture cannot be broken." The Greek word (luthēnai) means to be dissolved, undone, invalidated. Jesus is asserting that no word of Scripture can be set aside, overruled, or emptied of its authority. Every word is binding; every word is trustworthy; every word is the word of the unbreakable God.

This statement is especially remarkable because Jesus makes it in a polemical context: His opponents are about to stone Him for blasphemy, and He cites an obscure psalm in His own defense, and rests His entire argument on the inerrancy of a single word. The most controversial claim (that He is the Son of God) He defends by an appeal to the precision of Scripture. If even the details of a minor psalm are "unbreakable," then the whole of Scripture is established on the same foundation. B. B. Warfield observed that this is probably the strongest single statement of biblical inerrancy in the New Testament — and it comes from the lips of Jesus Himself.

verseByVerse.quote: For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and of spirit, of joints and of marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. — Hebrews 4:12
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer of Hebrews has been warning his readers against the hardness of heart that prevented the wilderness generation from entering God's rest (3:15–19), and he grounds the danger in the continuing power of the word of God. Scripture is not an ancient record of what God once said; it is the living word of the living God, still speaking, still piercing, still doing its work. The context implies that the Israelites who heard in the wilderness but did not believe were exposed to a word that was fully alive and fully powerful — and they hardened themselves against it to their destruction.

The sword metaphor is precise: "sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and of spirit, of joints and of marrow." The word penetrates to the most hidden, most interior parts of human experience — it reaches places that no human analysis can reach. And it does so not to harm but to discern: to expose the "thoughts and intentions of the heart" so that they can be brought to God for forgiveness and transformation. This is why Scripture reading and preaching are not optional extras in the Christian life but the means by which the Spirit does His searching, sanctifying work. The word is alive — it does things that human words cannot do, because it carries the authority and power of the God who breathed it out.

verseByVerse.quote: ...no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own interpretation. For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit. — 2 Peter 1:20–21
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter's phrase "carried along" (Greek pheromenoi) is evocative — it is used in Acts 27:15, 17 for a ship being driven by the wind. The ship moves; it goes where the wind takes it; but the ship's own structure and materials are still fully present. This is the perfect metaphor for verbal inspiration: the human authors were genuinely carried by the Spirit, moved by a power not their own, going where God directed; yet they wrote in their own styles, with their own vocabularies, out of their own experiences. The result is doubly authored: fully human and fully divine.

The origin of prophecy is negative and positive: negatively, it does not come from human will or human interpretation (the prophets did not invent what they said); positively, men spoke from God as they were carried along. The source is God; the instrument is the human author; the product is God's own word in human words. This is why the church has always read the Old Testament as the word of God to the present generation and not merely a record of ancient religious experience: it came from God through Spirit-carried human speakers, and it still comes from God to Spirit-illumined human readers.

verseByVerse.quote: Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path. — Psalm 119:105
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Psalm 119's world, walking without light meant stumbling on uneven ground, missing the path, falling into hidden ditches. The word of God functions as a lamp: not as a floodlight that illumines everything simultaneously, but as a lamp — giving enough light for the next step, enough clarity for the immediate path, enough guidance for the present decision. This is the pastoral function of Scripture's authority: not to answer every theoretical question but to guide the daily walk of the person who is committed to living for God in the concrete situations of real life.

The psalm as a whole (176 verses) is a sustained meditation on the worth, the beauty, the delight, and the life-giving power of God's word. The psalmist does not merely submit to Scripture reluctantly, as to an authority he would rather not have. He delights in it (v.14, 16, 24, 35, 47, 70...), meditates on it day and night (v.97), loves it with a passion (v.97: "Oh how I love your law!"). This is the Reformed vision of scriptural authority at its best: not a cage that constrains human freedom but a lamp that illumines the path to genuine flourishing, given by the God who knows us, loves us, and has spoken to guide us home.
